children.name: Testudo
children.description: The Mediterranean tortoises — the classic domed, high-shelled land tortoises of southern Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Testudo species have been kept as pets for centuries and were traded extensively across the ancient world; Roman soldiers carried them as a food source on campaign. All are under significant conservation pressure from habitat loss, collection for the pet trade, and the slow reproductive rate typical of long-lived reptiles.

children.name: Testudo graeca
children.description: The Greek tortoise, also known commonly as the Moorish tortoise and the spur-thighed tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The species is a medium-sized herbivorous testudinid, widely distributed in the Mediterranean region.

children.name: Testudo kleinmanni
children.description: Kleinmann's tortoise (Testudo kleinmanni), also called commonly the Egyptian tortoise, Leith's tortoise, and the Negev tortoise, is a critically endangered species of cryptodire turtle in the family Testudinidae. The species is native to Libya and possibly extinct in Egypt. The species was once more widespread, but its numbers are now dwindling, and complete extinction in the wild is a looming threat unless more actions are taken to protect this species.

children.name: Agrionemys
children.description: A monotypic genus containing Horsfield's Tortoise — the only tortoise of the Central Asian steppes, named after the naturalist Thomas Horsfield. Unlike its Mediterranean relatives it inhabits semi-arid grasslands and spends much of the year in torpor: active for only two to three months in spring, it spends the rest of the year in deep burrows escaping both summer heat and winter cold. It is the most widely kept tortoise in the world.

children.name: Agrionemys horsfieldii
children.description: Agrionemys horsfieldii (Horsfield's Tortoise) is a central asian tortoises species found in Asia region.

children.name: Kinixys
children.description: Hinged-back tortoises of sub-Saharan Africa — unique among tortoises in possessing a rear hinge on the carapace that allows the back of the shell to be lowered to protect the hindlimbs. Several species reach the savanna and open woodland at the southern edge of the Palearctic zone and are among the most ecologically diverse of African tortoises.

children.name: Kinixys erosa
children.description: The forest hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys erosa), also known commonly as the serrated hinge-back tortoise or Schweigger's tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The species is indigenous to the tropical forests and marshes of central and western Africa.

children.name: Kinixys belliana
children.description: Bell's hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys belliana), also known commonly as Bell's eastern hinged tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The species is native to central Africa. It has the hinge that characterizes all tortoises in the genus Kinixys. There are no recognized subspecies.

children.name: Kinixys homeana
children.description: Home's hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys homeana) is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The species is endemic to Africa.

children.name: Kinixys lobatsiana
children.description: The Lobatse hinge-back tortoise or Lobatse hinged tortoise (Kinixys lobatsiana) is a species of turtle in the family Testudinidae. It is found in Southern Africa.

children.name: Kinixys natalensis
children.description: The Natal hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys natalensis), also known as Natal hinge-backed tortoise or Natal hinged tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae which is restricted to eastern southern Africa to a relatively small area around the borders of Mozambique, South Africa, and Eswatini.

children.name: Kinixys nogueyi
children.description: Distributed across West Africa from Senegal to Ghana and into the Congo Basin, this species inhabits moist savanna and forest margins. It is morphologically similar to K. belliana but distinguished by a more rounded carapace and geographic distribution. Heavy exploitation for bushmeat markets and local traditional medicine poses significant conservation concern.

children.name: Kinixys spekii
children.description: Speke's hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys spekii), also known commonly as Speke's hingeback tortoise, is a species of turtle in the family Testudinidae. The species is endemic to Africa.

children.name: Kinixys zombensis
children.description: Described from the Zomba Plateau of Malawi, this species ranges through coastal East Africa from southern Somalia to South Africa. It inhabits coastal forest, thicket, and savanna, and is somewhat more arboreal in behaviour than other Kinixys, occasionally climbing low shrubs. It is Under Revised Taxonomy reclassified from K. belliana subspecies and remains poorly studied.

children.name: Geochelone
children.description: Large continental tortoises with a broad distribution across South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. The Indian Star Tortoise is named for the striking radiating yellow pattern on each scute — a pattern that breaks up the tortoise's outline in dappled grassland light and is among the most beautiful in the family.

children.name: Geochelone elegans
children.description: The Indian star tortoise (Geochelone elegans) is a threatened tortoise species native to India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka where it inhabits dry areas and scrub forest. It has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2016, as the population is thought to comprise more than 10,000 individuals, but with a declining trend. It is threatened by habitat loss and poaching for the illegal wildlife trade. It was upgraded to CITES Appendix I in 2019 by full consensus among all member states, giving it the highest level of international protection from commercial trade. Conservation group TRAFFIC found 6,040 were seized globally that were intended to be sold in the pet trade. Currently they are commonly bred in many countries to be sold as pets.

children.name: Geochelone platynota
children.description: The Burmese star tortoise (Geochelone platynota) is a critically endangered tortoise species, native to the dry, deciduous forests of Myanmar (Burma).

children.name: Aldabrachelys
children.description: A genus of giant tortoises from the western Indian Ocean, now represented by a single extant species on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles. Once distributed across Madagascar and other Indian Ocean islands, the surviving Aldabra giant tortoise is the world's largest land tortoise after the Galápagos species and one of the longest-lived animals on Earth.

children.name: Aldabrachelys gigantea

children.name: Centrochelys
children.description: A genus erected for the African spurred tortoise, the largest mainland tortoise on Earth and the third-largest tortoise species overall. Previously placed in Geochelone, it inhabits the arid Sahel belt of sub-Saharan Africa and is characterised by prominent spurred scales on the hindlimbs and a thick, yellowish-brown shell.

children.description: The African spurred tortoise (Centrochelys sulcata), also called the sulcata tortoise, is an endangered species of tortoise inhabiting the southern edge of the Sahara Desert and the Sahel.

children.name: Chelonoidis
children.description: South American and Galápagos tortoises — a diverse genus whose ancestors floated across the Atlantic from Africa to South America in the Oligocene. The genus includes some of the most iconic megafauna of the Western Hemisphere: the enormous Galápagos tortoises and the red- and yellow-footed tortoises of the South American rainforest.

children.name: Chelonoidis carbonarius
children.description:
The red-footed tortoise (Chelonoidis carbonarius) is a species of tortoise from northern South America. These medium-sized tortoises generally average as adults, but can reach over. They have dark-colored (nearly black), “loaf”-shaped carapaces (top shell) with a lighter patch in the middle of each scute (shell segment), and a somewhat lighter-colored plastron (underbelly). They also have dark limbs dotted with brightly-colored scales, from which they get their name, that range from pale yellow to vivid or dark red. Visible differences are noted between red-footed tortoises from varying eco-regions. They are closely related to the more easterly-distributed yellow-footed tortoise (C. Denticulatus) of the Amazon Basin.
Their natural habitat ranges from savannah to forest edges around the Amazon Basin. They are omnivorous tortoises, consuming a wide assortment of plants, grasses, flowers, fruit and (notably) fungi, as well as the occasional earthworm or other invertebrate. When presented with the opportunity, many tortoises will also scavenge on carrion. They do not brumate, due to their equatorial home range, but may aestivate in the hotter, drier months.

children.name: Chelonoidis denticulatus
children.description:
The yellow-footed tortoise (Chelonoidis denticulatus), also known as the Brazilian giant tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae and is closely related to the red-footed tortoise (C. Carbonarius). It is found in the Amazon Basin of South America. The species name has often been misspelled as denticulata, an error introduced in the 1980s when Chelonoidis was elevated to genus and mistakenly treated as feminine, an error recognized and fixed in 2017.
With an average length of 40 cm (15.75 in) and the largest known specimen at 94 cm (37 in), this is the sixth-largest tortoise species on Earth, after the Galapagos tortoise, the Aldabra tortoise, the African spurred tortoise (Geochelone sulcata, typical size 76 cm (30 in)), the leopard tortoise (Stigmochelys pardalis), and the Asian forest tortoise (Manouria emys), typical size 60 cm (23.6 in)).

children.name: Chelonoidis chilensis
children.description: The Chaco tortoise (Chelonoidis chilensis), also known commonly as the Argentine tortoise, the Patagonian tortoise, or the southern wood tortoise, is a species of tortoise in the family Testudinidae.

children.name: Chelonoidis abingdonii
children.description:
The Pinta Island tortoise (Chelonoidis niger), also known as the Pinta giant tortoise, Abingdon Island tortoise, or Abingdon Island giant tortoise, is a recently extinct subspecies of Galápagos tortoise that was native to Ecuador's Pinta Island.
The subspecies was described by Albert Günther in 1877 after specimens arrived in London. By the end of the 19th century, most of the Pinta Island tortoises had been wiped out due to hunting. By the mid-20th century, the subspecies was assumed to be extinct until a single male was discovered on the island in 1971. Efforts were made to mate the male, named Lonesome George, with other subspecies, but no viable eggs resulted. Lonesome George died on 24 June 2012, and the subspecies was believed to have become extinct with his death. However, 17 first-generation hybrids were reported in 2012 from Wolf Volcano on Isabela Island during a trip by Yale University researchers. As these specimens were juveniles, their parents might still be alive. The subspecies is classified as extinct on the IUCN Red List.

children.name: Chelonoidis becki
children.description: The Volcán Wolf giant tortoise (Chelonoidis niger becki), also known commonly as the Wolf Volcano giant tortoise and the Cape Berkeley giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The subspecies is native to the north side of Ecuador's Isabela Island (formerly Albemarle Island). Chelonoidis becki has links to two different lineages including that of Chelonoidis darwini from the nearby island of Santiago. C. Becki has been found to be the product of a double colonization event beginning around 199,000 years ago, and had been formed through introgression, where greater male selectivity was exhibited by purebred females in one of the lineages. It is most commonly found on the northern, western, and southwestern slopes of Volcán Wolf, the volcano that it is named for. Having evolved to live in a specific environment, C. Becki only occupies an estimated range of about 263 square kilometers. An estimated 1,150 Volcán Wolf giant tortoises inhabit Volcán Wolf.

children.name: Chelonoidis chathamensis
children.description: Chelonoidis niger chathamensis, commonly known as the Chatham Island giant tortoise or the San Cristóbal giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos.

children.name: Chelonoidis darwini
children.description: The Santiago Island giant tortoise (Chelonoidis niger darwini), also known commonly as the Santiago giant tortoise and the James Island tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise in the family Testudinidae. The subspecies is endemic to Santiago Island (also known as James Island and San Salvador) in the Galápagos.

children.name: Chelonoidis duncanensis
children.description: Chelonoidis niger duncanensis, commonly known as the Pinzón Island giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to Pinzón Island in the Galápagos.

children.name: Chelonoidis guntheri
children.description: Chelonoidis niger guentheri, commonly known as the Sierra Negra giant tortoise or Günther's giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to the Galápagos archipelago in the eastern Pacific Ocean. The specific epithet guentheri honours zoologist Albert Günther.

children.name: Chelonoidis hoodensis
children.description: The Hood Island giant tortoise (Chelonoidis hoodensis), also known commonly as the Española giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise native to Española Island in the Galápagos.

children.name: Chelonoidis microphyes
children.description: Chelonoidis niger microphyes, also known as the Volcán Darwin giant tortoise, Darwin Volcano giant tortoise or Tagus Cove giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to the Galápagos archipelago in the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean. The specific epithet microphyes is based on the mistaken assumption by describer Albert Günther that the holotype specimen (with a carapace length of only 57.2 cm) was of an adult male.

children.name: Chelonoidis phantasticus
children.description: Chelonoidis niger phantasticus is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise that was discovered in 1906 and thought extinct, until a single female was discovered living on Fernandina Island by an expedition in February 2019. In May 2021, a genetic test carried out by scientists from the California Academy of Sciences confirmed that the single female tortoise discovered in 2019 is from the subspecies Chelonoidis niger phantasticus. The subspecies name has often been misspelled as phantastica, an error introduced in the 1980s when Chelonoidis was elevated to genus and mistakenly treated as feminine, an error recognized and fixed in 2017.

children.name: Chelonoidis porteri
children.description: The western Santa Cruz tortoise (Chelonoidis niger porteri) is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos. They are found only on the southwestern slopes of the island, with an estimated range of 141 sq. Kilometers. There are approximately 3400 individuals in the wild, and have seen rising numbers in population, despite being critically endangered. MtDNA evidence shows that there are actually three genetically distinct populations on Santa Cruz Island. They are characterised by a black, oval carapace (to 130 cm) that is domed, higher in the centre than in the front, and broad anteriorly. Their life expectancy is 175 years. In 2015, the small, eastern Cerro Fatal population of the island was described as a distinct subspecies, C. N. Donfaustoi, most closely related to chathamensis (and forming a clade with it plus abingdoni and hoodensis), while the main southwestern porteri population was found to be closer to the Floreana and southern Isabela tortoises.

children.name: Chelonoidis vandenburghi
children.description: Chelonoidis niger vandenburghi, also known as the Volcán Alcedo giant tortoise, the Alcedo Volcano giant tortoise or the Alcedo giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to the Galápagos archipelago in the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean. The specific epithet vandenburghi honours American herpetologist John Van Denburgh.

children.name: Chelonoidis vicina
children.description: Chelonoidis niger vicina, commonly known as the Cerro Azul giant tortoise, Iguana Cove tortoise or the Isabela Island giant tortoise, is a subspecies of Galápagos tortoise endemic to Isabela Island in the Galápagos.

children.name: Chersina
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the angulate tortoise of southern Africa, one of the most common tortoises on the Cape Peninsula and the most abundant tortoise species in the Western Cape of South Africa. Its name derives from the Greek for 'of dry land', reflecting its preference for dry fynbos and Succulent Karoo habitats.

children.name: Chersobius
children.description: Tiny padloper tortoises of southern Africa — the smallest tortoises in the world. All three species were formerly placed in Homopus and are restricted to the arid and semi-arid regions of South Africa and Namibia. They are specialists of rocky outcrops and dwarf shrubland, and their flattened shells allow them to squeeze into narrow rock crevices.

children.name: Chersobius boulengeri

children.name: Chersobius signatus

children.name: Chersobius solus

children.name: Gopherus
children.description: The gopher tortoises of North America — powerful burrowing tortoises of the arid and semi-arid regions of the United States and Mexico, named for their extensive burrow systems that provide critical shelter for hundreds of other species. As ecosystem engineers and keystone species, gopher tortoises are among the most ecologically important reptiles on the continent.

children.name: Gopherus agassizii

children.name: Gopherus berlandieri

children.name: Gopherus evgoodei
children.description:
The Goode's thornscrub tortoise, also known as the Sinaloan thornscrub tortoise, Sinaloan desert tortoise or Goode's desert tortoise (Gopherus evgoodei), is a species of tortoise that is native to the Sinaloan desert region. First described in 2016, G. Evgoodei inhabits Tropical Deciduous Forest and Sinaloan Desertscrub biomes in Mexico. Its range may overlap in the north with G. Morafkai, the Morafka's or Sonoran desert tortoise.
Goode's thornscrub tortoise is named for Eric V. Goode, a conservationist, naturalist, and founder of the Turtle Conservancy.
children.authorship: Edwards, Karl, Vaughn, Rosen, Melendez-Torres & Murphy, 2016

children.name: Homopus
children.description: Small padloper tortoises of southern Africa, formerly encompassing the Chersobius species as well. The remaining Homopus species inhabit rocky succulent scrub in South Africa and southern Namibia, and are among the least studied tortoise genera due to their small size, secretive habits, and restricted distributions.

children.name: Malacochersus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the pancake tortoise — unique among tortoises for its remarkably flat, highly flexible shell. children.name: Manouria

Manouria is thought to be the most primitive living genus of tortoises based on molecular phylogenetics, retaining several ancestral skeletal features. Both species are Endangered and declining rapidly due to forest loss and consumption.

Each scute on their carapaces bears distinct radiating pale lines on a dark background, providing extraordinary camouflage among dry vegetation. All three species have limited distributions and face conservation challenges.

children.name: Pyxis
children.description: Two small, highly distinctive Malagasy tortoises — the spider tortoise and the flat-tailed spider tortoise — endemic to the arid southwestern coast of Madagascar. Both species have a remarkable hinge on the plastron (unusual in non-Kinixys tortoises) that allows females to close the front lobe over the limbs. Both are Critically Endangered.

children.name: Pyxis arachnoides

children.name: Pyxis planicauda
children.description:
The flat-backed spider tortoise (Pyxis planicauda), more commonly known as the flat-tailed tortoise, and Madagascan flat-tailed tortoise, is a tortoise that belongs to the family Testudinidae. The various common names for this small tortoise usually refer to the noticeably flattened nature of its oblong upper-shell or its tail.
The flat-backed spider tortoise is endemic to the west coast of Madagascar, between the Monrondava and Tsiribihina rivers. Due to the specifications of its habitat, the flat-backed spider tortoise is classified as critically endangered on the IUCN Red List.

children.name: Stigmochelys
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the leopard tortoise — the largest tortoise in Africa after the sulcata and one of the most widespread, occurring across sub-Saharan savannas from Sudan and Ethiopia south to the Cape. The leopard tortoise was placed in Geochelone for many years but molecular data confirms it forms its own distinct lineage.
